revisions.body: Apemantus supplies the comparison that starts the inquiry: he ranked the Iliad above the Odyssey because Achilles was better than Odysseus. Socrates reports that ranking and asks Hippias which man is better. At this point, I would not treat the passage as settling Socrates’ own verdict; the immediate task is to make Hippias state his.

revisions.title: From self-confidence to the false man’s power
revisions.body: Hippias’s confidence appears first as a boast, not as a title: since he began competing at Olympia, he says, he has met no one better in anything. He then distributes the superlatives: Achilles is bravest, Nestor wisest, and Odysseus wiliest. Socrates narrows the issue by asking what “wily” means. Hippias answers with Achilles’ truthfulness versus Odysseus’ falsity, then agrees that false men are powerful deceivers.
